tagline: Smoky foothills, storytelling tents and a lake above old Butler.
intro: The Great Smoky Mountains Byway follows the Smoky foothills, linking mountain scenery with towns and farms. Tennessee’s scenic-byways program identifies its scenic, recreational and historic qualities. On the U.S. 321 route through Townsend, two lanes cross rural Wears Valley before the road joins Pigeon Forge’s multilane strip of hotels and attractions. Farther along, U.S. 321 follows the national park’s northern boundary between Gatlinburg and Newport. The byway organization presents the wider journey as a tour of mountain landscapes, historic downtowns and local culture across seven Tennessee counties.

In the 1950s and 1960s, interstate construction brought I-75 and I-40 to the Lenoir City area. U.S. 321 was built through Lenoir City in the 1980s chiefly to improve access to Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Its Tennessee River crossing changed again in 2017, when a bridge southeast of Fort Loudoun Dam was completed.

Begin at Lenoir City and head through Maryville. State byway directions continue through Sevierville to Gatlinburg; this drive follows U.S. 321 through Townsend and Wears Valley to Pigeon Forge and Gatlinburg. Beyond Gatlinburg, follow the park’s northern edge through Cosby toward Newport, then continue through Greeneville, Jonesborough and Elizabethton. The final stretch winds between Pond Mountain and Watauga Lake.

moments.title: Townsend
moments.text: Townsend grew beside a sawmill in Tuckaleechee Cove. W.B. Townsend incorporated the Little River Lumber Company in 1901, and a railroad carried its wood products to market. People involved with the company chartered the city in 1921. As conservationists pressed to halt logging, Townsend sold 76,000 acres in 1926 for what became Great Smoky Mountains National Park. The town now serves as one of the park’s three gateways. Its Little River Railroad and Lumber Company Museum recounts the logging history that preceded that change. The railroad’s route followed the Little River, connecting the sawmill with Walland to the west and the mountain community of Elkmont upstream.

moments.title: Jonesborough
moments.text: Large tents turn Jonesborough’s parks into storytelling venues for the National Storytelling Festival. The International Storytelling Center holds the festival on the first full weekend of October, building on Appalachian storytelling traditions. The town dates to 1779, when this was part of North Carolina, seventeen years before Tennessee statehood. The historic district entered the National Register in 1969. Among its surviving buildings is the Chester Inn, built in 1797 and still standing downtown. The older Christopher Taylor House began outside town in 1777 and was later relocated into the historic district.

moments.title: Watauga Lake
moments.text: Watauga Lake covers the original town of Butler. TVA began the dam in 1942, halted work for other wartime projects and resumed in 1946. Completed in 1948, the dam impounded the Watauga and Elk rivers. Before the reservoir filled, Butler moved to higher ground. The relocation required new roads, three bridges and the movement of 1,281 graves. U.S. 321 now winds along the lakeshore, with Pond Mountain rising to the south. In 1983, a temporary drawdown exposed Old Butler’s remains, allowing former residents to revisit the place the reservoir had covered.
